title: Dirichlets Unit Theorem Regulators and S Units

items.title: Finitely many roots of unity in a number field
items.statement: Let K be a number field. The group μ(K) of roots of unity contained in K is finite.
items.strategy: A root of unity ζ∈K satisfies ζ^N=1 for some N≥1, so it is an algebraic integer (a root of the monic X^N−1); its minimal polynomial over Q lies in Z[X] and its degree [Q(ζ):Q] divides [K:Q] by the tower law, hence is at most [K:Q]. For each Q-embedding σ:K→C one has σ(ζ)^N=1, so |σ(ζ)|=1. Thus every root of unity in K is an algebraic integer of degree at most [K:Q] all of whose conjugates have modulus exactly 1. The batch-2 bounded-conjugates lemma leaves only finitely many monic integer polynomials of degree at most [K:Q] with all roots of modulus at most 1, and each such polynomial has at most [K:Q] roots; hence only finitely many algebraic integers, so finitely many roots of unity. This is the bounded-coefficients form of the design's 'bounded lattice points are finite' route: the finite integer box replaces the bounded lattice region; the argument itself introduces no Choice use and the item makes no standalone ZF claim.

items.title: Kronecker root-of-unity criterion
items.statement: Let K be a number field and let 0≠α∈O_K be an algebraic integer all of whose complex conjugates satisfy |σ(α)|≤1. Then α is a root of unity.
items.strategy: The norm Nm(α) is a nonzero integer and equals the product of the conjugates, so 1≤|Nm(α)|≤1 forces |Nm(α)|=1 and every conjugate has modulus exactly 1. Hence every power α^m is again an algebraic integer of degree at most n=[K:Q] whose conjugates σ(α)^m all have modulus 1. The bounded-conjugates lemma therefore allows only finitely many minimal polynomials, each with at most n roots, so the set {α^m : m≥1} is finite; two distinct powers coincide, and α≠0 gives α^{k−m}=1. Thus α is a root of unity. This is Milne's Corollary 5.6 and Stein's Lemma 8.1.8; the finiteness argument itself introduces no Choice use.

items.title: A number-field unit is exactly an algebraic integer of norm ±1
items.statement: For u∈O_K, u is a unit of O_K if and only if N_{K/Q}(u)=±1.
items.strategy: If u is a unit with inverse v∈O_K, then Nm(u)Nm(v)=Nm(uv)=1 with both factors in Z, so Nm(u)=±1. Conversely let |Nm(u)|=1 and fix one embedding σ₀. Then β=∏_{σ≠σ₀}σ(u) satisfies uβ=±1; β is a product inside K of conjugates of an algebraic integer, each integral over Z, hence β is an algebraic integer lying in K, i.e. β∈O_K by definition of the ring of integers as the integral closure of Z in K. Therefore u is invertible in O_K. Milne Lemma 5.2 and Stein Prop. 8.1.4; the argument itself introduces no Choice use. The converse direction is the one the unit theorem consumes, and it never passes through the norm being a unit in a larger ring.

items.title: Product formula for a number field
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a number field K normalize the finite absolute values by |x|_𝔭=N𝔭^{−v_𝔭(x)} for the nonzero prime ideals 𝔭 of O_K, the real ones by |x|_σ=|σ(x)| for the real embeddings, and the complex ones by |x|_τ=|τ(x)|^2 for one embedding from each complex pair. Then ∏_v|x|_v=1 for every x∈K^×, the product being over a finite set of places (the remaining factors equal 1).
items.strategy: Write x=a/b with a,b∈O_K\{0}, so (x)=(a)(b)^{−1} as fractional ideals. The plan requires the proved CA-9 interface and never the recorded ZF factorisation item: rings of integers are Dedekind domains, and the Dedekind unique-factorisation theorem writes (a)=∏𝔭^{e_𝔭} and (b)=∏𝔭^{f_𝔭} as finite products of prime powers. Hence v_𝔭(x)=e_𝔭−f_𝔭 vanishes outside the finite union of the two prime supports, and the contributing finite places are exactly that finite set. Multiplicativity of the ideal norm gives ∏_𝔭 N𝔭^{−v_𝔭(x)}=N(b)/N(a), and the principal-ideal norm formula N((α))=|Nm(α)| turns this into |Nm(b)|/|Nm(a)|=1/|Nm(x)|. On the archimedean side |Nm(x)|=∏_σ|σx|·∏_τ|τx|^2 by the embedding formula for the norm, and multiplying the two identities gives the product formula. The finite-prime step is the only Choice use: the CA-9 Dedekind ideal-class/unique-factorisation route records full Choice and NT-23 makes no standalone ZF claim (design, proof-strategy and choice section); the separately published ZF ideal-factorisation item is not substituted for the proved CA-9 supplier.

items.title: Logarithmic embedding of a number field
items.statement: Let K be a number field of signature (r₁,r₂), and fix one embedding τ_1,…,τ_{r₂} from each complex conjugate pair. The logarithmic embedding is λ:K^×→R^{r₁+r₂}, λ(x)=(log|σ₁x|,…,log|σ_{r₁}x|,2log|τ₁x|,…,2log|τ_{r₂}x|). The factor 2 on the complex coordinates is part of the convention and is not optional; real coordinates carry no factor.
items.strategy: The signature lists the embeddings and the log is defined on the positive moduli of nonzero values. Complex conjugates of a chosen embedding have equal modulus, so replacing τ_j by its conjugate does not change λ; the ordering of coordinates is auxiliary. Taking the doubled complex coordinate is what makes the product-formula hyperplane the literal coordinate-sum-zero hyperplane in the next item and what fixes the determinant normalization of the regulator; mixing the doubled and undoubled conventions silently multiplies covolumes by powers of 2.

items.title: Unit logarithms lie in the trace-zero hyperplane
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let H={(x_i)∈R^{r₁+r₂} : Σ_i x_i=0}. Then λ(O_K^×)⊆H; that is, the coordinate sum of λ(u) is log|Nm(u)|, which vanishes for every unit.
items.strategy: For a unit u the finite valuations v_𝔭(u) all vanish, since (u)=O_K; the product formula therefore collapses to ∏_σ|σu|·∏_τ|τu|^2=1. Taking logarithms (log of a product is the sum of the logs, log1=0) gives Σ_real log|σu|+Σ_complex 2log|τu|=0, exactly the coordinate sum of λ(u). Equivalently the coordinate sum is log|Nm(u)| and |Nm(u)|=1 by the unit criterion. Doubling the complex coordinate is what makes the sum literal, matching the design's convention. The Choice carried by this item is exactly the product-formula route's; the alternative direct derivation of the same identity from the embedding norm formula is recorded in the batch notes but is not the design route.

items.title: Kernel of the unit logarithm is the roots of unity
items.statement: ker(λ|O_K^×)=μ(K), the group of roots of unity contained in K; in particular the kernel is finite and is the torsion subgroup of O_K^×.
items.strategy: For λ(u)=0, each real and chosen complex embedding has modulus 1; every omitted complex conjugate has the same modulus by the complex modulus law, so Kronecker gives u∈μ(K). Conversely, a root of unity maps to zero because every embedding preserves its power equation. The kernel is finite by the roots-of-unity finiteness lemma and equals the torsion subgroup by the finite-order definition.

items.title: Discrete subgroups of a real vector space are lattices
items.statement: Let V be a finite-dimensional real vector space with the topology induced by a norm (equivalently V≅R^n), and let Γ≤V be a subgroup. The following are equivalent: (a) Γ is discrete in the induced topology; (b) every bounded subset of V meets Γ in a finite set; (c) Γ=Zv₁⊕···⊕Zv_r for some R-linearly independent v₁,…,v_r∈V, r≤dim V; that is, Γ is a lattice in V.
items.strategy: For (a)⇒(b), isolate 0 and cover each bounded set with a finite coordinate grid whose cells have norm diameter below the isolation radius; use norm equivalence and the reciprocal Archimedean bound, with no sequence selection. For (b)⇒(c), reduce modulo the integer span of a maximal independent tuple to a bounded parallelepiped. The resulting finite set F surjects onto Γ/Γ₀, so Lagrange embeds Γ in Γ₀≅Z^r after scaling. Induction on r, using only the cyclic-subgroup-of-Z result, gives a basis of the embedded subgroup; its real span forces its length to be r and its vectors to be R-independent. All selections are finite.

items.title: The logarithmic unit image is discrete
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. The subgroup λ(O_K^×)⊂H is discrete; equivalently, every bounded subset of H meets λ(O_K^×) in finitely many points.
items.strategy: By the (a)⇔(b) half of the lattice criterion lemma it suffices to show that every bounded C⊂H meets the image finitely. Let M bound the r₁+r₂ coordinates of points of C. If λ(u)∈C then |log|σu||≤M and |2log|τu||≤M, so e^{−M}≤|σu|≤e^M and e^{−M/2}≤|τu|≤e^{M/2}: every conjugate of u has modulus at most R=e^M. Each such u is an algebraic integer of degree at most [K:Q]; the bounded-conjugates lemma gives finitely many candidate monic integer polynomials and the root bound finitely many roots of those, so only finitely many units u occur. No injectivity of λ is claimed or needed — units differing by an element of ker λ=μ(K) have equal images, by the kernel lemma — and since the preimage λ^{−1}(C) is finite, so is its image C∩λ(O_K^×). This is Milne's proof of Prop. 5.8 and Stein's Lemma 8.1.9. The finiteness argument itself is elementary; the AC carried by this item is inherited through the hyperplane lemma's placement of the image inside H (product-formula route).

items.title: The logarithmic unit image is a full lattice
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. The discrete subgroup λ(O_K^×)⊂H spans H over R; hence it is a full lattice in H of rank r₁+r₂−1.
items.strategy: Follow Stein’s proof of Theorem 8.1.2 in the doubled-coordinate convention. Define A=√|d_K|(2/π)^{r₂} in Given before its first use; F14 establishes A>0 from the nonzero discriminant, positivity of π, and the positive square-root theorem. If the image spans a proper subspace W⊊H, choose z∉H⊥ and set f(x)=⟨z,λ(x)⟩, whose complex coefficient is 2z_{r₁+j}. For positive c_i with ∏real c_i∏complex c_{r₁+j}²=A, the product of real intervals and complex discs has volume 2^{r₁}π^{r₂}A, justified from the Countable-Choice-qualified box and Jordan/Lebesgue results followed by finite product-measure iteration. Equality-case Minkowski gives a nonzero a with |N(a)|≤A; lower and upper embedding bounds and bounded-norm ideal finiteness give a fixed finite generator list and a unit u. With t_c=Σreal z_i log c_i+Σcomplex z_{r₁+j}log(c_{r₁+j}²), rescaling two unequal weights makes |t_c| exceed the uniform bound, forcing f(u)≠0. Thus W=H; discreteness and the lattice criterion finish. Choice is declared through Minkowski, the product-formula/discreteness inputs, and the measure suppliers.

items.title: Dirichlet unit theorem
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a number field K of signature (r₁,r₂) there is an isomorphism O_K^×≅μ(K)×Z^{r₁+r₂−1}. In particular O_K^× is finitely generated of rank r₁+r₂−1 and its torsion subgroup is μ(K).
items.strategy: The logarithmic embedding restricts to a group homomorphism O_K^×→Λ=λ(O_K^×) with kernel μ(K). By the full-lattice theorem Λ is a free abelian group of rank r₁+r₂−1, so O_K^× is an extension of a finitely generated group by a finite group, hence finitely generated; its torsion subgroup is μ(K), because a unit of finite order is a root of unity. The structure theorem for finitely generated abelian groups decomposes O_K^× as its torsion subgroup times a free group of rank r₁+r₂−1 (the rank is additive in the exact sequence). The splitting is not canonical; it depends on the choice of generators, and rank and torsion do not. All Choice here is inherited through the previous item.

items.title: System of fundamental units
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let K be a number field with unit rank r=r₁+r₂−1. A system of fundamental units is a tuple (ε₁,…,ε_r) of units of O_K such that λ(ε₁),…,λ(ε_r) is a Z-basis of the unit lattice λ(O_K^×). Equivalently, every unit u admits a unique expression u=ζε₁^{m₁}···ε_r^{m_r} with ζ∈μ(K) and m_i∈Z. Such tuples exist by the unit theorem, and a system is an auxiliary choice, not canonical field data.
items.strategy: The equivalence of the two descriptions is the splitting O_K^×≅μ(K)×Z^r established in the unit theorem together with the fact that λ is injective modulo μ(K). Existence is inherited from the AC-qualified unit theorem; the tuple is noncanonical and two systems are related by a matrix in GL_r(Z). This item fixes the objects the regulator determinant is computed from.

items.title: Regulator of a number field
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let (ε₁,…,ε_r) be a system of fundamental units of K, r=r₁+r₂−1, and let A be the (r₁+r₂)×r matrix whose columns are λ(ε₁),…,λ(ε_r) in the doubled convention. For k=1,…,r₁+r₂ let A_k be the r×r matrix obtained by deleting row k. The regulator of K is the positive real number R_K:=|det A_k|; for r=0 the empty determinant is defined to be 1, so R_Q=1 and R_K=1 for imaginary quadratic K.
items.strategy: The deleted-row matrix is r×r; its determinant is well defined by the determinant of a square matrix. The definition names a deleted row because the columns lie in the hyperplane H, so every choice of row gives the same absolute determinant. The full-lattice theorem gives an R-basis of H, and any other Z-basis of the lattice differs by GL_r(Z), which ensures the chosen fundamental units also give R-independent columns. Independence of the fundamental system and the deleted row is the content of the next theorem. The empty determinant handles rank zero, and the doubled complex coordinates fix the normalization.

items.title: Deleted-row minors of a zero-column-sum matrix agree up to sign
items.statement: Let m≥1 and let A be an (m+1)×m real matrix of rank m each of whose columns has coordinate sum zero. Let Δ_k be the determinant of the m×m matrix obtained by deleting row k, for k=1,…,m+1. Then Δ_k≠0 and Δ_k=(−1)^{k−1}Δ₁ for every k; in particular all |Δ_k| are equal.
items.strategy: Put c_k=(−1)^{k−1}Δ_k. For each column index j, expand along the last column the determinant of the (m+1)×(m+1) matrix whose first m columns are those of A and whose last column is the j-th column of A; two columns are equal, so the determinant is zero, and cofactor expansion along the last column gives Σ_k (−1)^k a_{kj}Δ_k=0, i.e. A^Tc=0. The all-ones vector also satisfies A^T·1=0 because each column of A sums to zero. Transposition interchanges rows and columns, so rank A^T equals rank A = m (row rank = column rank), and rank-nullity gives nullity(A^T)=(m+1)−m=1; since the all-ones vector lies in ker A^T, that kernel is exactly the line it spans. The vector c is nonzero by the nonzero-minor criterion for rank m: some m×m minor is nonzero, i.e. some Δ_k≠0, and c_k=(−1)^{k−1}Δ_k. Hence c=λ(1,…,1) for some λ≠0, which is the claimed sign pattern and nonvanishing. No Choice is used.

items.title: The regulator is well defined
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. The regulator R_K is independent of the deleted row and of the chosen system of fundamental units, and R_K>0. Consequently R_K is an invariant of K (in the doubled logarithmic normalization), with R_K=1 for rank zero.
items.strategy: The columns λ(ε_i) lie in H and are R-linearly independent because they are a Z-basis of the full lattice λ(O_K^×); hence A has rank r, and the deleted-row lemma gives Δ_k=(−1)^(k−1)Δ_1, all nonzero, so |det A_k| is independent of k. For a second fundamental system, write λ(ε_iʹ)=Σ_j b_{ji}λ(ε_j), and let B=(b_{ji}) have the new basis coordinates as its columns. The reverse basis change also has integer coefficients, so B∈GL_r(Z); because the vectors are columns, Aʹ=AB and Aʹ_k=A_kB. The integer inverse makes det B a unit of Z, hence ±1, and determinant multiplicativity preserves each absolute deleted-row determinant. Thus R_K is independent of both choices and positive; Choice is inherited from the unit theorem.

items.title: Unit ranks by signature
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. The unit rank r₁+r₂−1 is 0 exactly for K=Q and for imaginary quadratic fields, and it is 1 for every real quadratic field; in general it equals r₁+r₂−1. The rank-0 cases have O_K^×=μ(K) finite and the rank-1 real quadratic case has O_K^×≅μ(K)×Z with μ(K)={±1}.
items.strategy: Read off signatures: Q has (1,0) and imaginary quadratic fields have (0,1), both giving rank 0; conversely r₁+r₂−1=0 forces r₁+r₂=1, so either r₁=1,r₂=0 (degree 1, hence Q) or r₁=0,r₂=1 (n=2 and nonreal, an imaginary quadratic field). A real quadratic field has (2,0), rank 1. The displayed unit groups come from the unit theorem; in the rank-1 case the torsion subgroup of a real field is {±1}. This is the design's rank table; it does not claim that rank 1 characterizes real quadratic fields (complex cubic and quartic fields also have rank 1 and are handled by the general formula).

items.title: S-integers and S-units
items.statement: Let K be a number field and let S be a finite set of nonzero prime ideals of O_K (only finite primes belong to S). The ring of S-integers is O_{K,S}={x∈K : v_𝔭(x)≥0 for all nonzero primes 𝔭∉S}, and the group of S-units is O_{K,S}^×={x∈K^× : v_𝔭(x)=0 for all 𝔭∉S}. No infinite place belongs to S: the archimedean places are already carried by the logarithmic embedding.
items.strategy: Valuations at nonzero primes are defined on fractional ideals; for x∈K^× one uses v_𝔭(x):=v_𝔭((x)), the principal fractional ideal. The displayed sets are a ring and its unit group (localisation at the multiplicative set generated by elements of K that are units at all primes outside S). The convention that S contains no infinite place is deliberate and matches Neukirch's Cor. (11.7): there S is a finite set of prime ideals of O_K with no infinite places, and with r,s the numbers of real and complex places the rank is #S+r+s−1, exactly r₁+r₂−1+|S| here. Infinite places never enter S; their contribution is already built into the logarithmic embedding.

items.title: S-unit theorem
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let K be a number field of signature (r₁,r₂) and let S be a finite set of nonzero prime ideals of O_K. Then O_{K,S}^×≅μ(K)×Z^{r₁+r₂−1+|S|}; in particular the S-unit group is finitely generated of rank r₁+r₂−1+|S| with torsion subgroup μ(K).
items.strategy: Let h be the class number of K, finite by the class-group finiteness theorem, and for 𝔭∈S let [𝔭] be its class in Cl(O_K); by Lagrange's theorem [𝔭]^h=1, so 𝔭^h=(π_𝔭) is a principal fractional ideal for some π_𝔭∈K^×, and v_𝔭(π_𝔭)=hδ_{𝔭𝔭}. The valuation map φ:O_{K,S}^×→Z^S, u↦(v_𝔭(u))_{𝔭∈S} is a homomorphism because valuations of products add; its image contains hZ^S and hence has finite index; its kernel is exactly O_K^×, since vanishing at every 𝔭∈S in addition to the definition's vanishing outside S is precisely being a unit. Therefore O_{K,S}^× is finitely generated (kernel and image are) of rank (r₁+r₂−1)+|S|, and its torsion subgroup is μ(K): a finite-order element of K^× is a root of unity and every root of unity satisfies v_𝔭(ζ)=0 whenever 𝔭 is a finite prime. The structure theorem for finitely generated abelian groups then yields the displayed isomorphism, which is noncanonical in the same way as the unit theorem's splitting.

items.title: Units of Q and the imaginary quadratic fields
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For K=Q: O_K=Z and O_K^×={±1}. For K=Q(i): O_K=Z[i] and O_K^×={±1,±i}=μ₄. For K=Q(√−3): O_K=Z[(1+√−3)/2] and O_K^×=μ₆={±1,±ω,±ω²} with ω=(1+√−3)/2. All three unit groups are finite of rank 0.
items.strategy: In each case the ring of integers is known and a unit is exactly an element of norm ±1. For Z the units are ±1; for Z[i] the norm is a²+b² so a²+b²=1 leaves the four Gaussian units; for Z[ω] the norm is a²+ab+b² and the six elements of μ₆ have norm 1 while the norm equation allows no others. Rank zero is the signature computation r₁+r₂−1=0+1−1=0, and the groups are the torsion groups μ(K), finite by the roots-of-unity result. Milne Example 5.3 and Sutherland Example 15.15.

items.title: Real quadratic units and Pell's equation
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let d>1 be squarefree and K=Q(√d). If d≡2,3 (mod 4) then O_K=Z[√d], and the unit group is ±⟨u_d⟩, where u_d is the least positive solution of the negative Pell equation x²−dy²=−1 when that equation is solvable, and u_d=ε_d is the fundamental Pell solution of x²−dy²=1 otherwise; in the solvable case ε_d=u_d² and the norm-one Pell subgroup ±⟨ε_d⟩ has index 2 in O_K^×. If d≡1 (mod 4) then O_K=Z[(1+√d)/2] strictly contains Z[√d]; the unit group of the order Z[√d] is as above, while the fundamental unit of O_K may be a half-integer element solving x²−dy²=±4 that does not lie in Z[√d], in which case Z[√d]^× (in particular the norm-one Pell subgroup ±⟨ε_d⟩) is a proper subgroup of O_K^×. For d=5 the fundamental unit of O_K is ε=(1+√5)/2 (norm −1), so O_K^×={±ε^n:n∈Z}, while in Z[√5] one has 2+√5=ε³, the fundamental Pell solution is ε₅=9+4√5=ε⁶, and Z[√5]^×=±⟨2+√5⟩=±⟨ε³⟩ has index 3 in O_K^×.
items.strategy: For units u_d and ε_d of the Pell order, u_d²=ε_d^n with n≥1. If n is even, equality of squares in the domain makes u_d=±ε_d^(n/2), contradicting its norm −1, so n is odd. If n≥3, write n=2m+1 and set w=u_d ε_d^−m. Both factors are units of Z[√d], so w remains in the Pell order; w²=ε_d, u_d=w^n, and w>1. Multiplicativity and N_d(u_d)=−1 force N_d(w)=−1. Writing w=x+y√d, its conjugate is −1/w, so x=(w−1/w)/2>0 and y=(w+1/w)/(2√d)>0. Since u_d=w^n>w, the increasing function t↦(t−1/t)/2 gives x smaller than the first coordinate of u_d, contradicting the least-positive choice. Thus n=1 and ε_d=u_d². If negative Pell is unsolvable, every Pell-order unit has norm +1 and the positive Pell solutions give ±⟨ε_d⟩. For d≡1 mod 4, maximal-order units solve x²−dy²=±4 and can lie outside the Pell order. For d=5, enumerate small y to see ε=(1+√5)/2 is the least maximal-order unit greater than 1; rank one gives O_K^×=±⟨ε⟩, while Z[√5]^×=±⟨ε³⟩ has index 3.

items.title: Two independent units in a real cubic field
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let α=2cos(2π/9), the root in (1,2) of f(X)=X³−3X+1. Then K=Q(α) is a totally real cubic field (r₁=3, r₂=0), so the unit rank is 2. The elements α (norm −1) and α−1 (norm 1) are units of O_K whose logarithmic vectors λ(α),λ(α−1)∈H are linearly independent over R; hence ⟨α,α−1⟩ is a rank-2 subgroup of O_K^× of finite index, confirming the rank.
items.strategy: The polynomial f is monic with no rational root, hence irreducible, and f(−2)<0<f(−1), f(0)>0>f(1), f(1)<0<f(2) locate three distinct real roots, so K has three real embeddings. For a monic cubic with roots α₁,α₂,α₃ one has Nm(α)=α₁α₂α₃=f(0)·(−1)³=−1 and Nm(α−1)=∏(α_i−1)=(−1)³f(1)=1, so both are units. Independence is checked exactly, not numerically: suppose α^m(α−1)^n=±1 for integers m,n; applying the three real embeddings, the value at σ₁ is positive, at σ₂ it has sign (−1)^n (since 0<α₂<1 and α₂−1<0), forcing n even, and at σ₃ it has sign (−1)^{m+n} (both factors negative), forcing m+n even, hence m even as well; dividing the relation by its square root α^{m/2}(α−1)^{n/2}=±1 and repeating gives m=n=0 by infinite descent. Thus λ(α),λ(α−1) are R-independent and generate a rank-2 subgroup of the rank-2 group O_K^×, i.e. a finite-index subgroup. The example deliberately claims only two independent units, not a full generating set: the Conrad text's displayed generators for this field fail a norm check (α+1 has norm −3 and is not a unit), so only the design's stated conclusion (two independent units, rank verified) is asserted.

items.title: Regulator of a real quadratic field
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a real quadratic field K=Q(√d) with fundamental unit ε>1 one has R_K=logε (doubled-complex convention, here vacuous). For K=Q(√5), ε=(1+√5)/2 and R_K=log((1+√5)/2)≈0.481212; the norm-one Pell generator 9+4√5=ε⁶ satisfies log(9+4√5)=6R_K, so using the Pell generator of the order Z[√5] as if it were the fundamental unit would multiply the regulator by six.
items.strategy: Here r₁=2, r₂=0, so r=1 and λ(ε)=(log|σ₁ε|,log|σ₂ε|)=(logε,−logε) because Nm ε=±1; deleting either of the two rows gives the 1×1 determinant logε up to sign, so the absolute value is logε, and ε>1 makes it positive. For d=5 the unit ε=(1+√5)/2>1 is fundamental (Example ex-real-quadratic-units-and-pell) and ε⁶=9+4√5, so the logarithms are in ratio 6; this exhibits concretely why the maximal order's unit, not a generator of the nonmaximal order Z[√5], defines the field invariant. Milne's regulator definition and Sutherland's Example 15.17 give R_K=logε for real quadratic fields.

items.title: A unimodular change of generators preserves the regulator determinants
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. With α=2cos(2π/9) the root in (1,2) of X³−3X+1 and u₁=α, u₂=α−1 the two independent units of the cubic example, the tuples (u₁,u₂) and (u₁u₂,u₂) generate the same lattice in H and every deleted-row 2×2 minor has the same absolute determinant for both tuples; numerically that common determinant is 0.849287…. The second tuple differs from the first by the unimodular integer matrix [[1,0],[1,1]] (columns), which illustrates the GL₂(Z) step in the well-definedness theorem; changing only the order of the two units changes the sign of the determinant and not its absolute value.
items.strategy: In log coordinates the second tuple is (λ(u₁)+λ(u₂),λ(u₂)), so its 3×2 matrix is A·C with C=[[1,0],[1,1]] (columns), det C=1; the deleted-row matrix transforms as A_k·C. Swapping u₁,u₂ uses C=[[0,1],[1,0]] with det −1. In both cases |det| is unchanged because det C=±1, and this is exactly the change-of-basis argument of the well-definedness theorem restricted to an explicit pair of tuples. The numerical value is checked from the three real embeddings 1.532088…, 0.347296…, −1.879385… and is displayed only as evidence; the invariance proved is exact.

items.title: S-units of Q
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let S={p₁,…,p_m} be a finite set of primes and let Z[S⁻¹] be the localisation of Z at the multiplicative set generated by S. Then Z[S⁻¹]^×={±p₁^{n₁}⋯p_m^{n_m} : n_i∈Z}≅{±1}×Z^m. This agrees with the S-unit theorem for K=Q, whose rank is r₁+r₂−1+|S|=0+m.
items.strategy: Every element of Z[S⁻¹] is a/b with b a product of primes from S (allowing b=1), and for p∉S the denominator b has v_p(b)=0, so v_p(x)≥0. If x is a unit then the same inequality applied to x⁻¹∈Z[S⁻¹] gives v_p(x)≤0 as well, hence v_p(x)=0 for every p∉S; unique factorisation in Z then writes x=±∏_{p∈S}p^{v_p(x)}. Conversely every such signed monomial lies in Z[S⁻¹] with inverse the opposite monomial. The abstract S-unit theorem for K=Q gives the same structure and rank |S|, and in the number-field dictionary the prime (p) is the finite prime of Q. The example is the design's explicit computation of U(S) for Q.

items.title: Units of Z[√5] are a proper subgroup of the units of its maximal order
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For K=Q(√5) one has O_K=Z[(1+√5)/2] and Z[√5]^×={±(2+√5)^n : n∈Z}={±ε^{3n}} with ε=(1+√5)/2, while O_K^×={±ε^n : n∈Z}; thus Z[√5]^× is a subgroup of index 3 in O_K^× and the two unit groups are not equal. The elementary Pell order cannot silently be identified with the maximal quadratic order.
items.strategy: The units of Z[√5] are the elements x+y√5 with Pell norm x²−5y²=±1. The norm-one integral solutions are ±ε₅^Z with fundamental Pell solution ε₅=9+4√5, and 2+√5 is the least positive norm-−1 solution, so the full unit group of the order is ±⟨(2+√5)⟩. In O_K, ε=(1+√5)/2 has norm ((1+√5)/2)((1−√5)/2)=−1, so it is a unit, and ε³=2+√5; the cubic example's group classification gives O_K^×=±⟨ε⟩. Hence Z[√5]^×=±⟨ε³⟩ has index [⟨ε⟩:⟨ε³⟩]=3 in O_K^× (the cube subgroup of Stein's §8.2.1 computation), and ε itself witnesses the inequality. This is deliberately the quantitative strengthening of the design's warning: it identifies both groups and the index rather than repeating the published NT-8 witness 'some unit of the larger order is missing from Z[√5]'.
